phonemes.desc: Short open [e] followed by nasal [n] — the Sumerian word for 'lord,' the title borne by every great deity.
Voiceless velar [k] and close front [i] — the Sumerian word for 'earth' or 'land,' here evoking the firm ground above the waters.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EN-kee' — two short, level syllables, with the crisp stop of the k between them.

kin.label: Sumerian
kin.form: 𒂗𒆠 (EN.KI), 'lord of the earth' — cuneiform title and theonym

kin.label: Akkadian
kin.form: Ea (𒂍𒀀), possibly from *hayy- 'life,' attested from the Old Akkadian period

kin.label: Logogram
kin.form: 𒀭𒂍𒀀 (dE-a), the divine determinative plus Ea

pronunciation.note: Enki is Tier 2 because the Sumerian name preserves neither stress in the Greek sense nor a contrastive long vowel in its conventional romanisation. The scholarly rendering with macron, Enkī, is sometimes used to mark an alleged length, but the cuneiform evidence points to a bisyllabic /ˈen.ki/; the Unicode form Enki is therefore the transparent, historically defensible primary spelling.

domains.title: The Sweet Waters of Wisdom
domains.subtitle: Abzu, Crafts, Incantations
domains.lead: Enki is the lord of the Abzu, the freshwater abyss that lies beneath the earth and feeds the springs, rivers, and marshes of Mesopotamia. He is not a sea-god; the sea is the domain of the unruly Tiamat. Enki's water is the sweet, creative water that makes civilization possible — the water that irrigates, cleanses, and inspires. Out of it he rises as the god of wisdom, magic, and the crafts that turn raw matter into culture.

cards.name: The Abzu
cards.desc: The subterranean freshwater ocean; Enki's temple at Eridu, the E-abzu, was built over it.

cards.name: Wisdom and Counsel
cards.desc: The god who knows the secret plans of the universe and whispers them to the righteous king.

cards.name: The Craftsman
cards.desc: Patron of exorcists, potters, smiths, and scribes; the divine engineer who devises solutions.

cards.name: Magic and Incantation
cards.desc: The ashipu-priest invokes Enki to undo sickness, demons, and the curses of fate.

symbols.name: Goat-fish (suhurmašu)
symbols.meaning: The hybrid sea-goat, Capricorn's ancestor, linking the Abzu with the stars

symbols.name: Flowing water
symbols.meaning: Streams issuing from his shoulders or a vase — life-giving freshwater

symbols.name: Tortoise
symbols.meaning: A creature of the marshy border between water and land, sacred to Enki

symbols.name: Eridu
symbols.meaning: His primordial city, the first city in Sumerian king lists and cosmology

symbols.name: Caduceus-like staff
symbols.meaning: The rod of magic and authority, sometimes twined with serpents

mythology.lead: Enki's myths are stories of intelligent intervention. He does not rule by force like Enlil or storm like Marduk; he solves problems, devises spells, and quietly redirects fate. His wisdom is practical, mischievous, and sometimes erotic — the wisdom of the craftsman who knows the properties of things.

myths.title: Enki and Ninhursag
myths.text: In the Sumerian myth Enki and Ninhursag, the land of Dilmun is a paradise without sickness or death but also without water. Enki impregnates Ninhursag, who gives birth to eight plants. When Enki eats the forbidden plants, Ninhursag curses him with eight ailments, one for each body part. She is later persuaded to heal him, creating eight deities from his afflicted limbs — a myth of botanical origin, sexual cosmogony, and the healing power that flows from the Abzu.

myths.title: Enki Warns Ziusudra
myths.text: In the Atrahasis epic and the Sumerian Eridu Genesis, the gods decide to send a flood to destroy humanity. Enki breaks the divine assembly's oath of silence and warns the pious king Ziusudra (later Utnapishtim) in a dream or through the reed wall of his house. Because of Enki, humankind survives; because of the flood, the gods learn that they need human labor. This is the earliest known flood narrative in world literature.

myths.title: Enki and the World Order
myths.text: In Enki and the World Order, the god assigns the me — the divine powers and offices of civilization — to the gods of Sumer. He establishes the Tigris and Euphrates, appoints the herding god, and regulates the sea, the winds, and the rains. The poem is a theodicy of culture: every institution has its divine origin in Enki's dispensation.

myths.title: Ea and Apsu in the Enuma Elish
myths.text: In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Ea (Enki) is the son of Apsu, the freshwater primal father, and Tiamat, the saltwater primal mother. When Apsu plots to destroy the noisy younger gods, Ea casts a spell and kills him, taking Apsu's place as ruler of the waters. His son Marduk will later defeat Tiamat. The pattern — older water-god supplanted by storm-god — parallels the Hittite Kumarbi-Taru and Greek Uranus-Kronos cycles.

lore.syncretism: Enki was identified with the Akkadian Ea, the Hurrian Kumarbi only in limited syncretistic contexts, and, across the ancient Near East, with water-and-wisdom deities generally. Greek writers later identified him with Poseidôn because of his aquatic domain, though Enki's freshwater wisdom is quite unlike Poseidon's saltwater tempests. In some Hellenistic and Gnostic currents, Ea/Enki was linked with Oannes, the fish-tailed culture-bringer described by Berossus. His iconography — water flowing from the shoulders — influenced later depictions of river gods and even of Saint Christopher in some Byzantine traditions.
lore.culturalLegacy: Enki survives most visibly in the figure of the wise craftsman-god: the deity who knows secrets and uses them to save rather than destroy. The flood story, transmitted through Atrahasis and the Epic of Gilgamesh, entered the biblical Noah narrative. The goat-fish became the constellation Capricorn. In modern speculative literature, Enki has been reclaimed as a figure of ecological wisdom, the patron of marshes and wetlands against the desert. The name still means: the intelligence that moves in deep water.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Enki teaches that civilisation begins not with conquest but with fresh water. Before there are laws, armies, or temples, there must be the spring that does not fail, the canal that reaches the field, the knowledge of how clay becomes brick and reed becomes basket. His domain is the Abzu — the hidden reservoir beneath the visible world — and his method is cunning rather than force.

In an age of ecological crisis, Enki is the god who matters most: the one who reminds us that wisdom is the art of fitting human life to the waters that sustain it. To restore the name Enki is to restore the sense that intelligence and nature are not opposites but allies, and that the deepest solutions often come from the quietest places.
